chapter: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
title: Hearing every part: playing Tyree Glenn's plunger parts with Ellington
summary: Hinton asks how he learned everyone's parts; Jackson says by listening, and tells how he covered Tyree Glenn's plunger book for Duke one night.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, you've always been such a great asset to every orchestra you've ever been with. I don't know whether you know it, brother, but you are considered amongst musicians a musician's musician, a complete musician. And any band or any group of musicians that get together and talk about sidemen or instrumentalists they refer to you as the most complete musician. You certainly are the most knowledgeable one for this background that you have. And I want to ask you about that. How did you come about -- I know I've worked with you in Cab's band and I've worked with you in studio recordings and whatnot and I know that you have the capacity to know everybody's part in the orchestra, not only your part but everybody else's part in the orchestra. And it has always been known that in Duke's band sometimes a guy would be late showing up. There was quite a bit of tardiness in the band. And you could take your trombone and play the alto part. How did you acquire that sort of a talent?

Just hearing, just listening, because I love to listen to parts. I love to listen to -- I love big bands. You know, I've never had the pleasure, really, to play with a small band but my ears I've always kept open and I like to listen to different parts, you know, different guys' parts, you know. That's how I come to play the plunger,
you see. Tyree wanted to go home. He wanted to come home to see Gloria once in Chicago --
Oh, that's when you were with Duke?

Yes. -- and so he goes to Duke and he never even asked me -- because you know how Tyree and I was, you know. We was very close, very, very close. People don't know, really, how close we were, you know. Tyree goes to Duke and I come to work the next night and here's this mute and plunger in front of my chair, and I said, "Oh, no." So Duke told me that, you know, "Tyree told me that you could play anything. So he told me that you could do this." And do you know that night he called Trans-Bluecency on me, he called Turquoise Cloud and all those things on me. I didn't even need to read the music because I heard every note Tyree played on those parts and I went out there and played it, --
-- you see? And you like to hear different saxophone parts. You know these parts, you see.
But most other people have never been able to do that. I notice that you, just from knowing you, I notice you hear, which is part of being a complete musician, you hear the whole band.
The whole [ ] of the band, which is
really what a musician should do.
